description:
Somos un equipo con una base sólida de ingeniería, pensamiento analítico y experiencia previa compitiendo y llevando ideas desde el concepto técnico hasta un prototipo funcional. Enfocados en que el equipo mantenga una estructura clara, datos respaldados por fuentes científicas y una propuesta de valor realista y bien fundamentada. Trabajando en entornos multidisciplinarios de investigación y competencias de innovación. 
"Un hombre puede soportar cualquier como, excepto la falta de sentido"
summary:
We built Gnomon, an open web tool that answers the four questions of the challenge for real Earth data: what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change can be told apart from natural variability. Users spin a 3D globe, pick a place and a variable, and get a plain-language verdict backed by four complementary statistical methods (Theil-Sen slope, autocorrelation-corrected Mann-Kendall, AR(1)-adjusted least squares and Newey-West HAC).

Gnomon covers 217 observed time series in 89 places and 8 themes, from rainfall in Nicaragua to Arctic sea ice, built on NASA GPM IMERG, GISTEMP, MODIS, SMAP, GLDAS, SWOT, OPERA and GRACE, plus CSA and NOAA records. All 13 challenge resources are in use, and 33 cross-checks compare independent products. The verdicts are honest: 79 trends detected, 85 with not enough evidence, 48 where methods disagree and 5 records too short to test.

A single straight line can be fooled by El Niño years, outliers and sensor changes. Gnomon shows the uncertainty, explains why "not enough evidence" never means "no change", and lets anyone download the data and check every number.
details:
Watch the 29-second demo

What exactly does it do?

Gnomon turns open satellite, model and station records into answers anyone can check. For every series it tells you what is changing, where, how much per decade, and how sure we can be. It covers 217 observed time series in 89 places and 8 themes: rain, temperature, vegetation and ecosystems, water bodies, air quality, coast and ocean, hurricanes, and ice.

  • Globe and map. A 3D globe with NASA GIBS imagery unfolds into a 2D map with radar, weather and watershed layers. Users can search any country or city.
  • Investigate. A three-step path (theme, place, variable) opens a verdict card: the change per decade with its 95% confidence interval, a plain-language answer to "how sure?", the time-series chart, published studies to compare against, and one-click CSV/JSON download.
  • Cross-checks. 33 side-by-side comparisons show when two independent products agree or not, for example GPM IMERG against CRU TS, GPCC and rain gauges, or SWOT lake levels against G-REALM altimetry.
  • Learn. Short visual lessons explain why months are not independent, what a confidence interval says, why "not enough evidence" is not "no change", and how to avoid false positives when testing many places at once.
  • Guided tours. Three tours start with a question, for example "Has Nicaragua's rainfall changed?" or "Is warming the same everywhere?", and teach users how to read the result and its uncertainty.

How does it work?

Each series with at least 10 years of data is tested by four methods at the same time:

  1. Theil-Sen slope with a 95% interval, robust to extreme years such as a hurricane or a strong El Niño.
  2. Mann-Kendall test with the Hamed-Rao correction, so that year-to-year persistence does not create false trends.
  3. Least squares with AR(1)-adjusted degrees of freedom (Santer et al., 2000).
  4. Least squares with Newey-West (HAC) errors, robust to autocorrelation and changing variance.

Only the statistical engine assigns a verdict. Trend detected (79 series) means all intervals exclude zero with the same sign and Mann-Kendall p < 0.05. Not enough evidence of a trend (85) means no interval excludes zero and p ≥ 0.05: the signal cannot yet be separated from natural variability. Methods disagree (48) warns about outliers, step changes or borderline cases. Records shorter than 10 years (5) are shown without a test. Gnomon detects change; it does not attribute causes, and each verdict holds only for the stated period and data product.

What does it find?

  • Mediterranean Sea, 1982-2025 (NOAA OISST): marine heatwave days rose by 22.6 days per decade (interval 6.2 to 35.0), and the sea surface warmed by 0.37 °C per decade. Trend detected.
  • Nicaragua's forests, 2001-2024 (Landsat, Hansen Global Forest Change): 20,231 km² of tree cover lost, 26% of the forest of the year 2000. On the Caribbean coast the loss reaches 33%.
  • North Atlantic hurricanes, 1980-2024 (IBTrACS): rapid intensification steps rise by about 2.1 per decade, but the interval runs from 0 to 4.4 and the methods disagree. Gnomon says so instead of hiding it.
  • Same 24 years, different answers: over 2001-2024 Nicaragua warms by 0.40 °C per decade, with an interval from +0.21 to +0.54 (trend detected), while the Canadian Prairies, with much larger year-to-year swings, show +0.18 °C per decade with an interval from -0.57 to +0.75 (not enough evidence). The difference is in the noise, not in the physics.
  • Rain in Nicaragua, 2001-2024 (GPM IMERG): -64.9 mm per decade with an interval from -233 to +98 mm. El Niño and La Niña drive large swings, and the tool explains why a longer record narrows the answer.

What benefits does it have?

  • Honest answers. Most tools stop at one regression line. Gnomon shows the uncertainty and says when the evidence is not there.
  • Verifiable. Every number can be downloaded and recomputed. Every published study shown has a DOI checked against Crossref.
  • For learners and decision makers. High-school and university students, teachers, science journalists and regional planners get short definitions, units and sources next to every result.
  • Local and global. It goes from a watershed in Nicaragua to Arctic sea ice with the same method, so users can compare regions fairly.
  • Open. Free, no login, available in English and Spanish, with light and dark themes and a mobile layout.

What makes it creative?

Gnomon treats disagreement as information. Instead of a single green or red light, it shows where four methods agree, where they do not, and why. It puts independent products side by side and catches data artifacts, such as a 2008-2013 jump in a land model that comes from a change in its input data, or a satellite warming signal that depends on the method, before they become false trends. The name comes from the rod of a sundial: around 240 BC Eratosthenes compared the shadows of a gnomon in two cities and measured the Earth. Gnomon follows the same idea: open data plus careful reasoning to tell real change from noise.

What do we hope to achieve?

We want anyone, from a student in Managua to a planner in the Sahel, to ask "is this really changing here?" and get an answer they can trust and check. Next steps: let users upload their own series or draw their own region, add more satellite variables through NASA Earthdata, and test the guided tours with classrooms and agricultural extension staff in Central America.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: JavaScript, HTML and CSS; Three.js (3D globe), Leaflet (2D map), Chart.js (charts), proj4js (coordinate systems).
  • Statistics and data: Python, NumPy, SciPy, FastAPI; reproducible downloaders for NASA, NOAA, CSA and partner archives; SHA-256 provenance checks.
  • Quality: an automated test suite (statistics, provenance and browser tests) and an accessibility audit against WCAG 2.2 AA criteria, documented in the repository (not a formal certification).
  • Hosting: Render (static site), GitHub (open source, Apache 2.0).

Team, prior work and AI

Team SpaceWheather (Managua, Nicaragua): Octavio Lizano, Benjamin, Astral, Manuel Paniagua and Javi. The 3D/2D weather viewer adapts components from the team's earlier project SICC-952; the trend engine, the 217 investigations, the cross-checks and the learning modules were built for Gnomon. We used AI assistants (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and Google Gemini) to speed up coding, data processing scripts, documentation and translation. No result is generated by AI: every number comes from the raw data through the statistical engine and is checked by automated tests. Full disclosure: docs/entrega/AI_USE.md in the repository.

Live app: https://nasa-challenge-q6cx.onrender.com/
Demo video (29 s): https://youtu.be/uy025KuxvBw
Source code (Apache 2.0): https://github.com/lizanooctavio-boop/NASA-CHALLENGE

Demo video: narrated by Benjamin in his own voice (no synthetic voice). The voice track was only trimmed, sped up by 5% and normalized. The video was assembled from real screen recordings of the live app with AI coding assistance (Claude Code); the animated rainfall chart and the verdict grid are drawn from the app data, and the sound effects were synthesized by the team.
